docs.title: Privacy Skill Vault
docs.text:
A personal cybersecurity portfolio, lab notebook, and practical knowledge base.

I work across cyber-fraud monitoring, security operations, and technical investigation. Privacy Skill Vault is where I document the concepts I study, the environments I build, the tools I test, and the investigation methods I refine.

The goal is straightforward: make technical work understandable, reproducible, and honest about what has actually been tested.

About me Explore the learning paths

docs.title: How information is labelled
docs.text:
Accuracy matters more than presentation. Content is identified by its evidence level:

  • Professional experience — generalised and sanitised descriptions; no employer, customer, or internal system details.
  • Lab-tested — performed in a controlled environment, with relevant setup and limitations recorded.
  • Simulated scenario — constructed for learning; not represented as a real incident.
  • Research note — based on documentation or external references and not yet independently validated.

docs.title: Current areas of focus
docs.text:
Cyber-fraud detection and investigation, SIEM monitoring, endpoint and network telemetry, detection engineering, Linux and Windows operations, and controlled security testing.

This is a personal learning and portfolio site. It does not represent an employer, disclose confidential operational information, or provide evidence of a real incident unless a page explicitly says so.

docs.title: About
docs.text:
I'm a cybersecurity professional working across cyber-fraud monitoring, fraud analysis, security operations, and technical investigation.

My current work focuses on monitoring fraud-protection systems, analysing suspicious activity, investigating alerts, tuning prevention controls, and supporting the reliability of security platforms. I also bring SOC analyst experience and continue to develop practical skills through structured study and controlled labs.

docs.title: Professional focus
docs.text:
• Cyber-fraud detection, prevention, and investigation
  • Account and transaction activity analysis
  • Security monitoring, alert triage, and escalation
  • SIEM workflows and detection tuning
  • Endpoint, network, and system telemetry
  • Security platform operations and troubleshooting

docs.title: Technologies and tools
docs.text:
Tools I have worked with or studied include Group-IB Fraud Protection, Elastic Stack, Splunk, Linux, Windows, PowerShell, Wazuh, Suricata, Zeek, Sysmon, Wireshark, Nmap, Burp Suite, and related security tooling.

This list is not a claim that every tool is used in production. Individual write-ups identify the environment and whether a technique was professionally used, lab-tested, or researched.

docs.title: Why this site exists
docs.text: I use this space to keep technical notes organised, record what worked and what did not, and turn isolated troubleshooting or investigation lessons into reusable references. The emphasis is on practical understanding rather than presenting a long list of tools or inflated claims.

docs.title: Responsible disclosure and privacy
docs.text:
Examples are sanitised or simulated. I do not publish customer data, account identifiers, internal IP addresses, employer-confidential information, or operational screenshots that could expose systems. Security testing content is intended only for systems you own or are explicitly authorised to assess.

For feedback or professional contact, use the public contact details linked from my professional profile.

docs.title: Blog
docs.text:
Technical articles and longer write-ups will be listed here when they are complete and reviewed.

The blog is separate from structured learning paths:

  • Learn explains concepts in a progressive sequence.
  • Labs records reproducible environments and experiments.
  • Investigations documents evidence-led analysis and worked scenarios.
  • Blog contains longer reflections, lessons learned, and technical deep dives.

New articles will be published on this domain so readers have one consistent destination. An empty publication list is better than linking to placeholder articles.

docs.title: Investigations
docs.text: Defensive investigation methods and worked examples covering security alerts, endpoint activity, network evidence, and cyber-fraud signals.

docs.title: Evidence standard
docs.text: Every report must distinguish observed evidence from interpretation. Published material is classified as sanitised professional experience, lab investigation, simulated scenario, or research note. No customer records, internal banking details, production IP addresses, or employer-confidential information belong here.

docs.title: Worked example: suspicious PowerShell launched by a scheduled task
docs.text:
SIMULATED TRAINING SCENARIO

Hostnames, timestamps, commands, and indicators in this example are synthetic. It does not describe a real customer, employer, or production incident.

docs.title: Initial alert
docs.text: A monitoring rule flags encoded PowerShell launched by a scheduled-task process outside an expected maintenance window.

docs.title: Investigation questions
docs.text:
1. What process created PowerShell, and what was its full command line?
  2. Which account and integrity level were involved?
  3. Is the scheduled task known, approved, and correctly owned?
  4. Do script-block, process, DNS, proxy, and firewall records corroborate the activity?
  5. Is there evidence of payload retrieval, persistence, lateral movement, or impact?

docs.title: Evidence to correlate
docs.text:
• Process creation telemetry, including parent process and command line
  • PowerShell operational events where logging is enabled
  • Scheduled-task registration and execution history
  • DNS and network connection records
  • File creation, hash, signature, and reputation context
  • Change records and owner confirmation

docs.title: Example reasoning
docs.text: An encoded command is a triage signal, not proof of malware. A scheduled task can be legitimate administration or unauthorised persistence. Validate the task definition, executable path, script contents, account, creation time, change history, and network destinations before assigning a verdict.

docs.title: Possible outcomes
docs.text:
• Expected administration: document the owner and maintenance purpose; tune narrowly with evidence.
  • Policy violation: remediate the configuration even if malicious intent is not established.
  • Likely compromise: follow incident-response procedures, preserve evidence, and consider containment under organisational policy.
  • Insufficient evidence: state what telemetry is missing and what additional collection is required.

Avoid treating one event or one indicator as a complete story. Record confidence, alternative explanations, data gaps, and the basis for every conclusion.

docs.title: Labs
docs.text:
Practical environments and experiments that connect cybersecurity concepts to observable system behaviour.

This section is documentation-led. A lab is described as tested only after the setup, versions, steps, and expected results have been verified. Proposed designs are reference architectures, not proof of running infrastructure.

docs.title: Infrastructure and platform
docs.text: Linux and Windows systems, virtual machines, virtual networking, storage, identity, and container fundamentals.

docs.title: Security monitoring
docs.text: A defensive stack can combine endpoint telemetry (such as Sysmon and Linux audit logs), network visibility (such as Zeek or Suricata), and central analysis (such as Elastic or Wazuh). Each integration should document resource requirements and data flow.

docs.title: Offensive security
docs.text: Isolated targets for reconnaissance, web application testing, vulnerability validation, and remediation verification. Testing remains within systems owned by the lab or explicitly authorised for assessment.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text: Repeatable tests for log generation, detection logic, parsing, network behaviour, platform troubleshooting, and security-control validation.

docs.title: Lab write-up standard
docs.text:
1. Objective, scope, and safety boundary
  2. Hardware, operating system, and software versions
  3. Architecture and network configuration
  4. Prerequisites and implementation steps
  5. Validation commands and expected results
  6. Observed output, issues, and troubleshooting
  7. Cleanup, rollback, and lessons learned
  8. References and last-reviewed date

A diagram or proposed tool list is not proof that an environment has been deployed. Each future write-up will state its status explicitly.

docs.title: Learn
docs.text:
A structured learning map for the technical foundations and security workflows covered by Privacy Skill Vault.

The curriculum is organised into five connected domains. Each domain will grow through concise explanations, tested examples, exercises, and references. A topic is not described as lab-tested until it has actually been validated.

D01Infrastructure & Platform FoundationNetworking, operating systems, virtualisation, cloud, and platform fundamentals. D02Security Monitoring & DetectionTelemetry, SIEM, alert triage, detection engineering, and threat hunting. D03Offensive Security & TestingAuthorised reconnaissance, web testing, vulnerability validation, and reporting. D04Security Operations & InvestigationsInvestigation methods, evidence correlation, incident response, and cyber fraud. D05Operations, Maintenance & CapstoneReliability, automation, operational change, validation, and integrated projects.

docs.title: How to use the learning paths
docs.text:
1. Start with the domain overview and prerequisites.
  2. Work through concepts before attempting the practical exercise.
  3. Record commands, versions, expected output, and observed results.
  4. Link the exercise to a lab or investigation where relevant.
  5. Revisit the references and note limitations or environment-specific behaviour.

Content status: These pages define the curriculum and study direction. Individual topics will be expanded as complete, reviewed material is ready; the site will not use placeholder cards to imply that unfinished guides are already published.

docs.title: D01 — Infrastructure & Platform Foundation
docs.text: Understand the systems and network services on which applications and security controls depend.

docs.title: Learning areas
docs.text:
• Networking: Ethernet, IPv4/IPv6, subnetting, routing, switching, VLANs, TCP/UDP, DNS, DHCP, HTTP/S, and TLS.
  • Linux: users and permissions, processes, services, storage, filesystems, logs, SSH, and systemd.
  • Windows: accounts, services, Event Viewer, PowerShell, process creation, and basic domain concepts.
  • Virtualisation and containers: hypervisors, virtual networks, images, containers, and resource allocation.
  • Platform operations: storage, CPU and memory, backups, patching, and availability.

docs.title: Practical exercise
docs.text: Build a small isolated network with one Linux system and one Windows system. Document the addressing plan, DNS resolution, connectivity tests, user permissions, service status, and relevant system logs.

docs.title: Evidence to record
docs.text:
Environment and software versions; network diagram and private lab IP plan; commands and expected results; troubleshooting and root cause; security implications and references.

D02 uses this foundation to understand telemetry. D04 uses it to correlate endpoint, identity, and network evidence.

docs.title: D02 — Security Monitoring & Detection
docs.text: Learn how security telemetry is collected, normalised, searched, correlated, and converted into actionable detections.

docs.title: Learning areas
docs.text:
• Log sources: Windows Security, Sysmon, Linux audit logs, firewall, DNS, proxy, web, and identity events.
  • SIEM foundations: ingestion, parsing, field mapping, timestamps, retention, searches, and dashboards.
  • Alert triage: context gathering, severity, scope, false positives, escalation, and documentation.
  • Detection engineering: Sigma concepts, rule logic, exclusions, testing, and change control.
  • Threat hunting: hypotheses, data requirements, pivots, baselines, and recording findings.

docs.title: Practical exercise
docs.text:
Generate benign process and authentication activity in a controlled endpoint. Confirm that expected events are collected, identify the fields needed for a detection, test a query against available data, and document false-positive conditions.

A rule is not production-ready merely because it parses or returns results. Record the data source, tested event samples, expected matches, false positives, performance considerations, and review date.

docs.title: D03 — Offensive Security & Testing
docs.text: Understand common attack paths so weaknesses can be identified, validated, explained, and remediated in authorised environments.

docs.title: Learning areas
docs.text:
• Scope, rules of engagement, asset discovery, and safe test planning
  • Reconnaissance and service enumeration
  • Web application fundamentals and common vulnerability classes
  • Authentication, session management, access control, and input handling
  • Vulnerability validation, evidence capture, impact assessment, and remediation
  • Retesting and clear technical reporting

docs.title: Practical exercise
docs.text:
Use an intentionally vulnerable local application. Define the scope, identify one low-risk finding, reproduce it without accessing real user data, capture minimal evidence, explain impact, recommend a fix, and retest.

Only test systems you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Avoid destructive payloads, production data, persistence, or unnecessary service disruption.

docs.title: D04 — Security Operations & Investigations
docs.text: Develop a repeatable approach to investigating suspicious activity using evidence from endpoint, network, identity, application, and fraud-monitoring systems.

docs.title: Learning areas
docs.text:
• Alert validation, triage, prioritisation, and escalation
  • Timeline construction and event correlation
  • Endpoint process, persistence, and authentication analysis
  • Network and DNS investigation
  • Threat intelligence: relevance, confidence, age, and context
  • Cyber-fraud patterns, account takeover signals, and transaction context
  • Incident handling, evidence integrity, containment considerations, and lessons learned

docs.title: Practical exercise
docs.text:
Use a synthetic alert dataset. Define the question, preserve original evidence, normalise timestamps, correlate related events, identify what is known and unknown, and write a conclusion with confidence and next steps.

Separate observed facts from assumptions. Record data-source limitations, time-zone handling, missing telemetry, alternative explanations, and confidence.

docs.title: D05 — Operations, Maintenance & Capstone
docs.text: Connect technical security work to stable, supportable operations.

docs.title: Learning areas
docs.text:
• Service health, capacity, storage, performance, and availability
  • Patch, configuration, and vulnerability management
  • Backup, recovery, disaster recovery, and change control
  • Automation with reviewable scripts and safe failure handling
  • Operational documentation, runbooks, escalation, and handover
  • Detection and platform maintenance, tuning, and regression testing

docs.title: Capstone approach
docs.text: Choose a small, authorised lab environment and define a measurable security objective. Build the environment, generate test activity, collect telemetry, implement a detection, investigate the result, tune false positives, document operational requirements, and demonstrate recovery or rollback.

docs.title: Completion evidence
docs.text: Scope, architecture, assumptions, reproducible setup and version details, test cases and observed results, security and operational risks, recovery procedure, and lessons learned.

docs.title: Privacy and external services
docs.text:
Most parsing, extraction, and transformation features process input locally in your browser. The Threat Intel Hub is different: it sends the single indicator you submit to public third-party services only after you select Enrich Indicator. IPv4 lookups use Shodan InternetDB and RDAP; domain lookups use RDAP and Cloudflare DNS. Optional links to VirusTotal, AbuseIPDB, URLScan, and Shodan also send the indicator to the selected provider when opened.

The Threat Intel Hub does not make requests while you type. Provider responses may be incomplete, unavailable, or out of date; they are not a verdict that an indicator is malicious or benign.

Do not paste customer information, authentication data, internal logs, confidential indicators, or employer-sensitive material into this public page. Public providers may process or retain submitted indicators under their own terms and policies. Review those policies before use.

docs.title: Operational limitations
docs.text:
• Tool output is an aid to analysis, not a verdict or automated security decision.
  • The Sigma page currently displays source YAML only. It does not parse or validate YAML, evaluate Sigma conditions, or generate Elastic, Splunk, or Sentinel queries. Use maintained Sigma tooling for conversion, then validate the result against your SIEM schema and telemetry.
  • CVSS scoring accepts CVSS v3.1 vectors, validates required Base metrics and supported metric values, and calculates Base, Temporal, and Environmental scores using the v3.1 equations. Confirm the vector and scoring assumptions before using the result in vulnerability prioritization.
  • Detection templates are examples and must be tested and reviewed before operational deployment.
  • Results can vary with browser support, input format, data quality, and external service availability.

Use only on data you are authorised to process.
